food.text: In the Arabian Peninsula, herding came long before farming. Animal husbandry first arose around 5500 BCE in the area of Oman, but agriculture did not arise until the early Bronze Age.

From the 3rd millennium BC, the straits of Hormuz and Bab-el Mandeb around the Arabian Sea were gateways for the region's first international trade networks. Along these routes travelled many things, including domesticate variants of crops and livestock, which spread across the Old World over millennia.

Oasis cities of the Hejaz, such as Yathrib (Medina) and Al-Ula, had regular access to water and became major trading cities as early as the Bronze Age. The domestication of the dromedary camel made long-distance trade possible for them.

The rise of the incense trade demanded the movement of incense, spices and other luxury goods from South Arabia into the Eastern Mediterranean. This trade passed through the Hejaz along the way, which helped its oasis cities grow rich.

art.text: Between about 2600 and 2000 BC, the Umm al-Nar culture of southeastern Arabia built circular tombs from well-fitted dressed stone. These tombs often held many individuals. The culture flourished in what is now the United Arab Emirates and northern Oman.

Along the Red Sea coastal plain of Yemen and southern Saudi Arabia, the Sabir culture raised standing stones known as menhirs. They are known from the Tihamah plain and are associated with ritual or territorial marking.
Rock art from the Bronze Age, beginning in the early 3rd millennium BCE, is sparse and harder to identify in Arabia. One of its few markers is the human figure carrying a lunate pommel dagger.

The Umm al-Nar culture is known not only for its tombs but also for large, tower-like settlement structures. Its stonework shaped both the places where people lived and the places where they buried their dead in southeastern Arabia around 2600 to 2000 BC.

The Wadi Suq culture (c. 2000 to 1300 BC) succeeded Umm al-Nar in southeastern Arabia and changed how tombs were built. Where Umm al-Nar tombs were large and circular, Wadi Suq tombs are elongated and rectangular, and they can be multi-chambered.

The Sabir culture, dated by excavations at Ma'layba and Sabir to between 1900 and 800 cal BC, built hut architecture in sedentary settlements. Its sites also show irrigation and layered habitation deposits, and archaeologists use its pottery styles to define its phases.

Burial sites of the Wadi Suq culture frequently contain soft-stone vessels with incised geometric designs. They also hold bronze daggers, swords and spears, as metallurgy became more advanced in southeastern Arabia.

Some Bronze Age rock art figures in Arabia are shown in what archaeologists describe as "bracket-like" or "lizard-like" postures. These distinctive poses help researchers pick out the few carvings from this period.
Bronze Age rock art in Arabia occasionally includes stylized cattle. These carvings also tend to show lighter varnish accumulation, which is another of the limited markers used to recognize them.

war.text: King Sargon of Akkad, who ruled from 2371 to 2316 BCE, boasted that his ports were home to boats from Tilmun, Magan and Meluhha. Akkadian campaigns against Magan took place in the twenty-third century, and Manishtusu and Naram-Sin both wrote of campaigning against '32 lords of Magan'. Naram-Sin, Sargon's successor, conquered Magan outright, and the towers built around wells in Magan may have been defensive against such attacks.
Dilmun was a Bronze Age civilization in eastern Arabia that covered Bahrain, Kuwait and eastern Saudi Arabia. It was conquered by the Middle Assyrian Empire beginning around 1365 BCE.

In the Wadi Suq period of southeastern Arabia, lasting from about 2000 to 1300 BCE, burial sites frequently contained bronze weapons such as daggers, swords and spears. This reflects more advanced metallurgy than in the earlier Umm al-Nar culture.
At Al-Khutm in modern Oman, dated to the 3rd millennium BCE Hafit period, ruins are thought to derive from a stone fort. The fort's tower was made of rock with a diameter of 20 metres.

literature.text: A Sumerian myth called the saga of Enki and Ninhursag described Dilmun as a paradise where predators did not kill, no one grew old, and there was no pain, disease, fear, or death. Dilmun covered the area of modern Bahrain, Kuwait, and eastern Saudi Arabia.

The earliest Sumerian written references to Magan, the Bronze Age name for a region in what is now Oman and the United Arab Emirates, date to the Umm al-Nar period between 2600 and 2000 BCE. These early texts also mention 'the Lords of Magan.'

The oldest known examples of the Ancient South Arabian script are painted pottery sherds from Raybun, in Hadhramaut, Yemen, dated to the late second millennium BCE. This abjad, in which only consonants are normally written, branched from the earlier Proto-Sinaitic script.

One of the earliest known inscriptions to mention Dilmun belongs to King Ur-Nanshe of Lagash, dated to around 2300 BC. Found carved into a door-socket, it records that 'the ships of Dilmun brought him wood as tribute from foreign lands.'

King Sargon of Akkad, who reigned from 2371 to 2316 BCE, boasted that his ports were home to boats from Tilmun, Magan, and Meluhha. Tilmun was another name for Dilmun, the region centered in modern Bahrain.
Modern theories often claim that the Sumerians regarded Dilmun as a sacred place. Yet no surviving ancient text actually says this, making it an assumption rather than a documented belief.

Trade between the Indus Valley and Sumer that passed through Magan was disrupted for a time. Around 2113 to 2096 BCE, King Ur-Nammu of Ur claimed in an inscription to have 'brought back the ships of Magan,' restoring the route.

Around 1370 BC, during the reign of Burna-Buriash II, a provincial official named Ilī-ippašra, stationed in Dilmun, wrote two letters to his friend Enlil-kidinni, the governor of Nippur. These letters, using Akkadian names throughout, suggest an administrative relationship between Dilmun and Babylon at the time.

A text discovered at Qal'at al-Bahrain names Ea-gamil, the last ruler of the Sealand dynasty, which is thought to have ruled Dilmun from at least 1500 BC. After his reign, control of Dilmun passed to the Kassite dynasty of Babylon.

science.text: In southeastern Arabia, the Wadi Suq culture (c. 2000 to 1300 BC) saw metallurgy become more advanced. Its burial sites often contain bronze weapons such as daggers, swords and spears. These finds show that metalworking skills were growing across the region.

The Umm al-Nar culture (c. 2600 to 2000 BC) of southeastern Arabia is known for circular tombs made of well-fitted dressed stone, often holding many individuals. It also built large, tower-like settlement structures. Its builders clearly had skill in shaping and fitting stone.

At Ras al-Jinz, on the easternmost point of the Arabian Peninsula, archaeologists found pieces of bitumen impressed with ropes, reed mats and wood planks. A few still had barnacles attached. This suggests the bitumen was caulking for an early boat.

Dilmun's system of weights and measures matched those used in the Indus Valley rather than those of southern Mesopotamia. This match reflects Dilmun's role as a trading hub linking Mesopotamia and the Indus civilization.

In 1982, a potsherd attributed to the Indus Valley Civilization was found at Ras al-Jinz. It was considered landmark proof that at least coastal Oman was connected to India in the third millennium BCE.

The straits of Hormuz and Bab-el-Mandeb served as gateways linking distant regions from the 3rd millennium BC, when the first international trade networks were established. Along these routes, technologies and other ideas spread widely across the Old World, as did domesticated crops and livestock.

Copper mining and smelting for the Dilmun trade network centered on the Umm al-Nar culture and the sites of Dalma and Ibri. The copper ingots produced were likely traded for cotton textiles and domestic fowl from the Indus region.

Wadi Suq tombs differ from those of the earlier Umm al-Nar culture. Where Umm al-Nar tombs were large and circular, Wadi Suq tombs are elongated and rectangular, and can have several chambers. Burials there also include soft-stone vessels with incised geometric designs.

Archaeologists studying Oman treat the amount of industry and manufacturing as a barometer of change between ages. They look especially at copper, which survives as slag, along with other metallic artifacts. Metalworking waste thus helps mark the shift from one age to the next.

Al-Natah, in the Khaybar Oasis of Saudi Arabia, was a walled Bronze Age town of about 1.5 hectares with some 500 residents, protected by ramparts. It was occupied from around 2400 to 1500 BCE. It may represent a transitional stage between mobile pastoralism and complex urban settlements.

Despite its irrigation and hut architecture, Sabir culture appears to have had mostly local social networks. Limited evidence exists for long-distance exchange between it and the core kingdoms of South Arabia. Its standing stones, called menhirs, are found on the Tihamah plain.

politics.text: Two letters found at Nippur, dated to the reign of the Kassite king Burna-Buriash II around 1370 BCE, mention Dilmun in eastern Arabia. They hint at an administrative relationship between Dilmun and Babylon at that time.
Assyrian inscriptions dated to 1250 BCE proclaimed the Assyrian king to be "King of Dilmun and Meluhha". Assyrian inscriptions of this time also recorded tribute from Dilmun.
By the Isin-Larsa Period, around 1900 BCE, Dilmun monopolized the trade with Meluhha. The Bahrain National Museum assesses that Dilmun's "Golden Age" lasted from about 2200 BCE to 1600 BCE.

The straits of Hormuz and Bab-el-Mandeb, at the edges of the Arabian Sea, have served as gateways linking the kingdoms and polities of the Old World's east and west. This role dates back to the first international trade networks of the 3rd millennium BC.

One of the Nippur letters was written by a provincial official in Dilmun named Ilī-ippašra to his friend Enlil-kidinni in Mesopotamia. The names in the letters are Akkadian, which points to close ties with Mesopotamia.

Akkadian campaigns against Magan took place in the twenty-third century, and both Manishtusu and Naram-Sin wrote of campaigning against '32 lords of Magan'. Naram-Sin not only conquered Magan but also honoured its king, Manium, by naming the Mesopotamian city of Manium-Ki after him.

After the Kassite dynasty collapsed, Mesopotamian documents stopped mentioning Dilmun, apart from Assyrian inscriptions dated to 1250 BCE. Those inscriptions claimed the Assyrian king ruled Dilmun and Meluhha.

Literary references to trade with Meluhha date from the Akkadian period, around 2300 BC, but the trade probably began in the Early Dynastic Period around 2600 BC. Some Meluhhan vessels may have sailed directly to Mesopotamian ports before Dilmun took over the trade.

Akkadian armies campaigned against Magan in the twenty-third century BCE, and Naram-Sin and Manishtusu both wrote of campaigning against '32 lords of Magan'. Naram-Sin conquered Magan, yet honoured its king, Manium, by naming the Mesopotamian city Manium-Ki after him. He also gave the defeated ruler of Magan the Akkadian title Malek, a term related to the Semitic and Arabic word for king, malik.

culture.text: Around 2600 to 2000 BCE, the Umm Al Nar people of what is now the United Arab Emirates and northern Oman acted as go-betweens for Sumer in Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley Harappan culture. The Sumerians called the area 'Magan' and drew copper and diorite from it, along with carnelian jewellery from the Indus.
During the Hafit period, from 3200 to 2600 BCE, people in southeastern Arabia built burial cairns that looked like beehives. Each held a small chamber for one or two burials.

The Wadi Suq period brought more inland settlement, increasingly sophisticated metallurgy and the domestication of the camel. Scholars now see the shift from the trading Umm Al Nar era as evolutionary rather than revolutionary.

Magan was famed for its shipbuilding and maritime skill. King Sargon of Akkad boasted that his ports were home to boats from Tilmun, Magan and Meluhha, and Ur-Nammu claimed to have 'brought back the ships of Magan'.

Wadi Suq people, living from 2000 to 1300 BCE, buried their dead in long chambers entered from the side, and many were reused for later burials. At Shimal in Ras Al Khaimah, over 250 burial sites survive, and in some cases cut stone from Umm Al Nar tombs was reused to build Wadi Suq graves.

As the water table dropped over the centuries between the Umm Al Nar and Wadi Suq periods, people moved toward the wetter areas around the Hajar Mountains. Known Wadi Suq burials cluster in the mountains of Ras Al Khaimah, Fujairah and Oman.

Dilmun, in Eastern Arabia, was central to the Sumerian creation myth. The saga of Enki and Ninhursag described it as a paradise where predators do not kill, people do not grow old, and disease and death are absent. The tale may have inspired the Garden of Eden story.

A pair of copper-alloy cymbals from the late third millennium BCE was found at the Dahwa 7 site in northern Oman. They lay carefully deposited inside a small ritual building, and they closely resemble examples from the Indus Valley civilization, suggesting musical practices travelled between regions.

Archaeologist Karen Frifelt linked the Hafit people to Sumer through distinctive Jemdet Nasr pottery found in their burials. She also mapped a field of some 400 graves in the Wadi Suq, inland of Sohar in Oman.

The Jebel Buhais burial ground is the oldest radiometrically dated burial site in the UAE. It contains a unique clover-leaf shaped Wadi Suq tomb, BHS 66, which stands as a one-of-a-kind piece of funerary architecture in the country.

The Sabir culture, along the Red Sea coastal plain of Yemen and southern Saudi Arabia, has phases dated between 1900 and 800 cal BC. It is known for hut-architecture, irrigation and menhirs on the Tihamah plain, associated with ritual or territorial marking.
